CHAPTER 1: INTRODUCTION
BACKGROUND OF THE STUDY
International university studies show that a Learning Management System (LMS) can
provide support for planning, monitoring, and reviewing learning alongside access to course
materials. Du et al. (2025) examined 69 management undergraduates taking mathematics at a large
public university in China, whose name was not disclosed. Students using its self-regulated learning
support reported stronger self-regulation; an examination advantage appeared on the first test but
not the second. Similarly, Çakiroğlu et al. (2024) studied a third-year Operating Systems and
Applications course at a public university in Turkey. They found significant associations between
assessment interactions and goal setting, self-evaluation, and help-seeking. The Chinese study
evaluated an intervention, whereas the Turkish study examined interaction patterns. Together, they
support considering how academic information and learning support work within the same
environment, without assuming that system access alone improves learning.
Research in computing education also indicates that engagement mechanisms need to serve
a defined instructional purpose. Ahmed et al. (2025) evaluated a gamified, mobile, cloud-based
LMS with 60 second-year students taking Object-Oriented Programming at Mansoura University in
Egypt. Their experimental group obtained higher post-test achievement and engagement scores than
the comparison group. In a broader systematic review, Jaramillo-Mediavilla et al. (2024) reported
favorable motivation and academic-performance findings in parts of the reviewed gamification
literature. The Mansoura study provides evidence from a specific computing course, while the
review draws together findings from multiple educational settings. These studies justify examining
participation support in an institutional LMS, but their educational results cannot be presumed for a
newly developed system at Colegio de Montalban.
In the Philippines, studies show that the organization of an LMS affects how students and
instructors experience academic tasks. Llamas et al. (2025) examined the Moodle-based LMS of
Mindanao State University–Iligan Institute of Technology in Iligan City through discussions and

task interaction involving six academics and six fourth-year students. They identified improvement
areas in usability, communication, course building, monitoring and assessment, content
management, and technical support. Laspiñas and Almerez (2024) surveyed 33 business graduate
students at an unnamed university in Cebu City and reported generally neutral task-related and
experience-related evaluations. The MSU–IIT study identified workflow concerns, while the Cebu
study described users’ overall experience. Both support examining clarity and usability through
actual academic tasks instead of treating the availability of a platform as sufficient evidence of its
suitability.
Within Colegio de Montalban, the present study focuses on the Institute of Computing
Studies (ICS), including the academic workflows of its students and instructors and the
administrative functions supporting them. Computing education requires coordination of learning
resources, coursework, programming activities, assessment records, and faculty responsibilities.
The research group’s initial project description identifies the use of separate tools for academic
work and personal organization as a concern to be addressed. This description serves as the starting
problem context, while the extent of fragmentation and users’ specific difficulties remain matters
for local requirements gathering.
The central development problem is how to organize these related activities within a shared
environment while maintaining clear responsibilities and appropriate access to information.
Students need understandable access to their coursework and academic records; instructors need
manageable teaching workflows; academic supervisors need suitable course-level information; and
administrators need controlled system-management functions. A connected design must also
account for schedules, changes in class occurrences, and the privacy of personal academic
information. Combining these responsibilities requires more than placing several tools on the same
screen.
In response, this study proposes the CdM Learning Management System (CdM LMS), a
multi-platform environment tailored to ICS. Its interconnected applications will provide

complementary access to shared information, with the Web Portal serving as the principal academic
environment, the Mobile Application supporting selected academic and productivity activities, and
the Desktop Application serving as the Administrator Console. The study will develop and evaluate
the system within the ICS setting. Its contribution will be evidence about the suitability and quality
of this institutional implementation, rather than an assumed improvement in students’ grades or
long-term learning outcomes.
STATEMENT OF THE PROBLEM
This study seeks to determine the level of software quality of the LMS for ICS at Colegio de
Montalban in supporting coordinated academic resource and grade management, learning support,
academic coordination, and system administration. The evaluation will follow six selected
characteristics of the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 Software Product Quality Model (International
Organization for Standardization [ISO], 2023).
Specifically, the study seeks to answer the following questions:
1. What is the level of the LMS in supporting academic resource and grade-management workflows
in terms of functional suitability, as measured by:
• Functional completeness in supporting course materials, assignments, dynamic grading,
CodeLab activities, Git-integrated submissions, and the defined academic coordination
functions;
• Functional correctness of weighted grade computations, EXP and level calculations,
descriptive analytics, and schedule revisions and exceptions;
• Functional appropriateness in supporting connected academic workflows for BSIT and
BSCpE users within their assigned roles and platform responsibilities?
2. What is the level of the system in providing understandable and engaging task interaction in
terms of interaction capability, as reflected in:

• Appropriateness recognizability of course, grading, productivity, gamification, and
academic coordination functions;
• Learnability of permitted tasks in the Web Portal, selected Mobile Application functions,
and administrator-only Desktop Application;
• User engagement supported by EXP, levels, achievements, leaderboards, study tools, and
the moderated Knowledge Exchange environment?
3. What is the level of the system in protecting academic information and controlling access in
terms of security, as demonstrated by:
• Confidentiality of student grades, personal notes, academic records, and restricted course
information;
• Integrity of grades, submissions, schedule records, and events during authorized updates
and concurrent actions;
• Accountability through activity and audit records for designated administrative actions,
academic coordination changes, and Knowledge Exchange moderation?
4. What is the level of the system in processing academic information and maintaining applicable
shared records in terms of performance efficiency, as indicated by:
• Time behavior in computing grades, generating descriptive analytics and calendar views,
retrieving course resources, and displaying relevant in-LMS updates;
• Resource utilization during the processing and retrieval of shared information by the
authorized Web, Mobile, and Desktop components under defined workloads?
5. What is the level of the system in providing stable access to permitted academic and study
functions in terms of reliability, as evaluated through:

• Availability of the Web Portal, supported mobile study tools, and Administrator Console
during the defined evaluation period;
• Fault tolerance when processing interrupted requests, concurrent grade updates, or
simultaneous Knowledge Exchange activity, including the handling of failed operations
without incomplete or duplicate records?
6. What is the level of the system in supporting consistent information exchange and operation
alongside other software in terms of compatibility, as indicated by:
• Interoperability among the Web Portal, Mobile Application, and Administrator Console
through their applicable shared records and authorized backend workflows;
• Co-existence of the Administrator Console with other software in the supported
administrator workstation environment without adversely affecting their operation?
OBJECTIVES OF THE STUDY
General Objective
To develop and evaluate a Learning Management System for the Institute of Computing Studies at
Colegio de Montalban that coordinates academic management, learning support, academic
oversight, and system administration through shared information and role-appropriate access.
Specific Objectives
The study specifically aims to:
1. Establish shared backend services and a centralized PostgreSQL database for the principal Web
Portal, complementary Mobile Application, and administrator-only Desktop Application, with
credential-based authentication, verified and approved accounts, and server-enforced access for
Student, Instructor, Super User, and Administrator roles.

2. Develop course and section management that allows authorized instructors to organize materials,
annotations, assignments, announcements, and deadlines, and allows enrolled students to access
resources and submit permitted work under the applicable validation rules.
3. Implement a Dynamic Gradebook with configurable assessment components and weights, score
recording, automatic weighted-grade computations, personal student grade views, instructor
performance summaries, and CSV grade export; verify computed values and charts against
documented test records.
4. Provide CodeLab for in-browser programming execution and assessment against predefined test
cases, and a separate Git-integrated workflow for repository-based coursework submission and
instructor review; verify the supported submission and access rules for each workflow.
5. Develop notes, task lists, flashcards, review and mastery records, focus timers, and study-session
tracking, together with rule-based EXP, levels, achievements, badges, streaks, and department
leaderboards; verify progression calculations and the separation of EXP from course grades and
forum reputation.
6. Implement Knowledge Exchange for academic questions, answers, and resource sharing, with
authorized instructor moderation, Faculty-Verified Answers, contribution-based reputation, and
records of designated moderation actions.
7. Develop the proposed faculty directory and academic operations hub, distinguishing program
affiliations and Dean or Program Head designations from primary account roles, and providing
restricted course supervision that excludes student identities, individual grades, submissions,
assessment attempts, and answers.
8. Implement Asia/Manila-based weekly course schedules with effective-dated revision history and
future occurrence cancellation, rescheduling, and restoration; provide authorized calendar views,
audience-targeted saved events, coursework deadlines, and private note–event snapshot conversion,
and verify their visibility and preservation rules.

9. Provide the Administrator Console with account approval, status and role management, permitted
configuration, activity and audit records, reporting, and the backup and recovery functions
supported by the evaluated release; verify that administrative permissions remain separate from
academic oversight.
10. Evaluate the developed system in terms of functional suitability, interaction capability, security,
performance efficiency, reliability, and compatibility using role-appropriate tasks, feedback from
eligible ICS students and instructors, and technical checks by qualified IT experts, and document
defects and limitations identified in the evaluated version.
CONCEPTUAL FRAMEWORK

The project developers adopted the Input–Process–Output (IPO) model as the conceptual
framework for the development of the proposed Learning Management System for the Institute of
Computing Studies (ICS). The IPO model consists of four main components: input, process, output,
and feedback, which provide a systematic approach for analyzing and developing information
systems. According to the Adobe Experience Cloud Team (2023), the IPO framework helps
organize system components by identifying required inputs, defining the development process, and
determining the expected outputs of the system. By applying the IPO model, the project developers
are able to clearly identify the necessary resources and requirements, structure the development
stages, and evaluate the outcomes of the system. In addition, the framework supports continuous
improvement by incorporating feedback from system users and evaluation results.
In the input phase, the project developers will gather all necessary information and resources
required for the development of the proposed system. These inputs include the review of related
literature (RRL), existing academic practices within the Institute of Computing Studies, and the
identified system requirements. The review of related literature serves as a significant secondary
source of information that helps the project developers understand the current developments and
challenges associated with Learning Management Systems in higher education. The literature
highlights key areas such as the utilization of LMS platforms in digital learning environments,
usability challenges encountered by users, student engagement and self-regulated learning in online
systems, digital assessment and academic monitoring tools, and the integration of emerging
technologies in educational platforms. These studies provide important insights that support the
rationale and objectives of the proposed system.
Furthermore, the project developers will examine the existing academic practices and
challenges experienced by ICS instructors and students in managing learning resources and
monitoring academic progress. Current practices often involve the use of multiple disconnected
platforms for distributing learning materials, managing assignments, calculating grades, and
communicating with students. The use of fragmented tools may result in inefficiencies, difficulty in

monitoring academic performance, and limited opportunities for collaborative learning. Through
the identification of these challenges, the project developers will be able to determine the necessary
features that should be integrated into the proposed system to improve academic productivity and
learning management.
Based on the gathered inputs, the project developers will propose the development of a
Learning Management System designed to provide centralized academic tools for both instructors
and students. The proposed system integrates several innovative features such as dynamic grading
and grade analytics, academic productivity tools including note-taking and task management,
communication tools such as announcements and chatbot assistance, gamification elements
including experience points and leaderboards, flashcard-based learning modules, and a knowledge
exchange forum that supports peer-to-peer collaboration. In addition, the system will incorporate a
Git-integrated submission engine that supports programming-related coursework and introduces
students to industry-standard version control practices commonly used in software development.
The development of the proposed system will utilize various technologies, tools, and
development platforms that support modern web-based application development. These include
computers and laptops used for system development and testing, as well as development tools such
as code editors, UI/UX design platforms, and version control systems that facilitate collaboration
among project developers. These technologies play an important role in ensuring that the system is
efficiently developed and capable of operating reliably across multiple platforms.
In the process phase, the project developers will follow the Agile software development
methodology to guide the development of the proposed Learning Management System. Agile
methodology emphasizes iterative development, collaboration, and continuous improvement
throughout the system development life cycle (Ling et al., 2022). The process includes six iterative
stages: planning, design, development, testing, deployment, and review. During the planning stage,
the system requirements and project objectives will be identified through analysis and consultation

with stakeholders. In the design phase, the developers will create system models, diagrams, and
interface prototypes to visualize the structure and functionality of the system. The development
phase will involve the actual coding and implementation of system modules and features based on
the approved design.
After development, the system will undergo comprehensive testing and evaluation to ensure
that all functionalities operate correctly and meet the required software quality standards. The
testing phase will involve identifying system errors, usability issues, and potential security
vulnerabilities. The system will be evaluated using the ISO/IEC 25010, which measures software
quality based on characteristics such as functional suitability, usability, reliability, security, and
compatibility. Once the system meets the required quality standards, it will proceed to the
deployment phase, where the system will be introduced to the intended users. The final stage of the
process is the review phase, where the system performance will be continuously monitored and
improvements will be implemented based on evaluation results and user feedback.
In the output phase, the expected result of the study is the successful development of a
Learning Management System that supports academic management, student engagement, and
collaborative learning within the Institute of Computing Studies. The system aims to provide a
centralized digital platform where instructors can manage course materials, monitor student
progress, and evaluate academic performance. At the same time, students will be able to access
learning resources, organize their academic tasks, collaborate with peers, and monitor their learning
progress. Through these capabilities, the proposed system aims to enhance digital learning
experiences and improve the overall efficiency of academic management within the institution.
The final component of the IPO model is feedback, which plays an essential role in ensuring
continuous system improvement. Feedback will be collected from system users, including students,
instructors, and IT experts, through system evaluation and usability testing. The feedback gathered

will allow the project developers to identify areas that require improvement, address potential
issues, and implement system enhancements in future updates. This continuous feedback loop
ensures that the proposed system remains responsive to the evolving needs of its users and
continues to effectively support digital learning environments.

OPERATIONAL FRAMEWORK
Figure 2
An Operational Framework Illustrating the Development of the Learning Management System Using the
Agile Model

The researchers adopted and customized the Agile software development model to guide the
development of the Colegio de Montalban Learning Management System (CdM LMS). Agile
methodology supports flexibility, collaboration, iterative development, and continuous
improvement throughout the software development process. Ling et al. (2022) explained that Agile
development enables development teams to work through iterative cycles, allowing adjustments and
continuous integration of feedback. Similarly, Laoyan (2025) emphasized that Agile practices
support effective system development by encouraging collaboration between stakeholders and
developers, which contributes to improved system quality and project outcomes.
Furthermore, Agile methodology allows system requirements and features to be refined
throughout the development process based on identified user needs and evaluation results. This
approach is relevant to learning management systems because their functionality, usability, and user
interaction may require continuous refinement during development (Zawacki-Richter et al., 2022).
Based on these principles, the researchers applied an iterative development process consisting of
Planning, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, and Review.
The project will follow an iterative Agile development approach consisting of planning,
design, development, testing, deployment, and review. Each cycle will address a manageable set of
requirements and produce a version that can be examined through relevant user tasks. Changes
identified during testing or review will be carried into subsequent work.
Planning Phase
During the Planning Phase, the researchers will identify and clarify the academic and
operational requirements of ICS at Colegio de Montalban. They will review the supplied project
specifications and gather local information about course resources, assignments, programming
activities, grade management, personal study, faculty coordination, and administrative
responsibilities. The requirements will cover BSIT and BSCpE without limiting the study to a
particular year level.

The researchers will define the responsibilities of Students, Instructors, Super Users, and
Administrators. They will establish the principal academic functions of the Web Portal, the selected
academic and productivity functions of the Mobile Application, and the administrative functions of
the Desktop Administrator Console. Academic designations, including Dean and Program Head,
will be distinguished from primary account roles. The planning process will also identify privacy
boundaries, ownership rules, and dependencies among the proposed modules.
The researchers will examine requirements for student productivity, participation, and
collaborative learning, together with the proposed faculty directory, restricted course supervision,
schedules, and audience-targeted events. The attention to both user tasks and institutional
responsibilities is informed by Llamas et al. (2025) and Guico (2026), whose studies identify
user-experience and institutional-support concerns in Philippine LMS settings. Local requirements
will determine how these concerns apply to ICS.
The identified requirements will be organized into a prioritized development backlog. Each
selected requirement will include expected behavior, permitted users, applicable platforms, and
acceptance criteria. The resulting requirements, role-and-platform access matrix, and development
priorities will guide the succeeding phases.
Design Phase
During the Design Phase, the researchers will translate the selected requirements into the
architecture, database relationships, system workflows, and user interfaces of CdM LMS. The
system will be designed as complementary Web, Mobile, and Desktop applications connected
through shared backend services and a centralized PostgreSQL database. The design will specify
how authorized records are created, updated, retrieved, and presented across the applicable
applications.

The researchers will prepare system flowcharts, an Entity Relationship Diagram (ERD), and
Data Flow Diagrams (DFD) based on the defined workflows and implementation requirements.
These models will identify the movement of academic information and the responsibilities of each
component. Grade computations, EXP progression, submission rules, calendar audiences, and
timetable revisions will have documented inputs, validation rules, and expected outputs.
The interfaces will reflect the tasks and permissions of their intended users. The Web Portal
will organize principal academic activities and the proposed coordination functions; the Mobile
Application will support selected academic and productivity tasks; and the Desktop Application
will support Administrator operations. Super User supervision will be designed around permitted
course-level information while excluding student identities, individual grades, submissions,
attempts, and answers.
The researchers will design understandable navigation, task labels, feedback, and
information organization. LMS user experience is relevant to this work because the Philippine
studies of Laspiñas and Almerez (2024) and Llamas et al. (2025) emphasize users’ interaction with
the platform. The design will therefore be examined through the tasks specified for each role. The
resulting interfaces, workflow models, data specifications, access rules, and test cases will guide
development.
Development Phase
During the Development Phase, the researchers will implement the selected requirements
according to the system designs. Development will proceed incrementally, allowing related modules
to be connected, checked, and refined before further functions are added. Applicable clients will
communicate with the documented Next.js backend and shared PostgreSQL database.
Authentication, validation, and authorization will be enforced through the supported backend
workflows.

Data and Reporting
• Permitted data-management functions;
• Supported CSV, JSON, and text exports;
• Printable PDF reports supported by the release;
• Supported backup and recovery workflows.
The researchers will verify the actual coverage of reporting, monitoring, exports, and recovery
before documenting them as completed functions. IBE and ITE configuration will remain a
technical capability outside the research population. Repository authorization will remain distinct
from credential-based LMS authentication, and CodeLab assessment will remain distinct from
repository-based submission review.
Each development increment will be checked against its acceptance criteria and connected to its
related records. Database constraints, transactions, and version checks will be applied where
specified to protect information during related or concurrent changes. The working increments will
then proceed to broader testing, with identified defects returned for correction.
Testing Phase
During the Testing Phase, the researchers will determine whether the developed functions
operate according to their documented requirements. Testing will examine functional behavior,
interfaces, access restrictions, record handling, cross-application consistency, and failure conditions.
Test accounts and controlled academic records will be used to compare actual outputs with expected
results.
The researchers will check weighted-grade computations, EXP and level calculations, descriptive
analytics, submission validation, deadline restrictions, and CodeLab test outcomes. They will also
examine faculty-directory permissions, restricted supervision, effective-dated timetable revisions,

future class exceptions, event audiences, and note–event snapshot conversion. Attempts to access or
change prohibited information will be tested using the relevant roles.
Integration checks will examine the applicable information shared by the Web Portal,
Mobile Application, Desktop Administrator Console, and database. Technical checks will measure
response time and resource use under defined workloads, inspect failure handling and record
consistency, and examine the Administrator Console’s co-existence with other software on
supported administrator workstations. Relevant in-LMS updates will be tested according to
implemented behavior, without assuming external push delivery or instantaneous synchronization.
The testing and evaluation criteria will follow the six selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023
characteristics identified in the Statement of the Problem: Functional Suitability, Interaction
Capability, Security, Performance Efficiency, Reliability, and Compatibility (ISO, 2023). Technical
results will be distinguished from respondent ratings. Defects will be recorded, corrected, and
retested, while unresolved limitations will be documented before the affected version is made
available for evaluation.
Deployment Phase
During the Deployment Phase, a reviewed CdM LMS version will be configured in a
controlled environment representative of its intended use. The researchers will prepare the Web
Portal, selected Mobile Application functions, and Desktop Administrator Console according to
their defined responsibilities. They will configure approved test accounts, role permissions, sample
academic records, and user guidance.
The researchers will verify backend connectivity, supported startup procedures, and
available data-continuity functions before users perform evaluation tasks. They will record the
release version, enabled modules, supported platforms, and known limitations so that evaluation
findings can be attributed to the system actually examined.

The deployed evaluation version will allow eligible users to perform permitted academic,
study, coordination, or administrative tasks. This controlled release will support the collection of
task feedback and technical observations. It will not establish institution-wide adoption or the
completion of proposed functions that have not yet passed implementation and testing.
Review Phase
During the Review Phase, the researchers will examine testing results, software-quality
ratings, technical observations, and user feedback. Eligible ICS students and instructors will
perform tasks appropriate to their permissions, while qualified IT experts will examine relevant
technical and administrative functions. The review will determine which acceptance criteria have
been met and which issues require correction.
The researchers will summarize the evaluation results using the descriptive procedures
specified in Chapter 3. They will relate reported difficulties and technical findings to the six
selected quality characteristics without treating favorable ratings alone as proof of calculation
correctness, security, or fault tolerance. The review will document supported behavior, unresolved
defects, and practical limitations of the evaluated version.
The findings will be prioritized and returned to the development backlog. Requirements,
interfaces, or implementation will be revised in the next cycle where necessary, and corrected
functions will undergo further testing. This use of feedback reflects the iterative improvement
described by Laoyan (2025). The Review Phase will therefore produce evaluation findings, an issue
list, and updated priorities for aligning the system with the academic and operational requirements
of ICS.

SCOPE AND LIMITATIONS
The study will cover the development and evaluation of CdM LMS for ICS at Colegio de
Montalban. Its academic context includes BSIT and BSCPE within ICS, without restricting
participation to a particular student year level. Department configuration for IBE and ITE is a
technical capability of the application; those institutes are outside the research population and the
intended generalization of findings.
The applications will use complementary responsibilities. The Web Portal will provide the
principal environment for academic workflows and the proposed academic coordination functions.
The Mobile Application will provide selected academic and productivity functions for students and
instructors according to their permissions. The native Desktop Application will be dedicated to
Administrator operations. The Super User will access academic oversight through the web
environment and will not use the native Administrator Console. Additional Administrator access
through web or mobile is not assumed.
The functional coverage includes academic and course management, grading and descriptive
analytics, programming activities, collaborative learning, personal study and organization tools,
gamification, academic coordination, and system administration. The feature groups and their
user-facing behavior are described in Section 1.8. The expanded coordination coverage includes
faculty relationships, read-only course supervision, recurring schedules with effective-dated
revisions, exceptions affecting individual class occurrences, targeted events, and private
note–calendar snapshot conversion.
The evaluation will use a quantitative descriptive approach and criterion-based purposive
sampling involving ICS students, ICS instructors, and qualified IT experts.
A student respondent should:
1. Be officially enrolled in the Institute of Computing Studies of Colegio de Montalban;

4. Have sufficient familiarity with software systems or Learning Management Systems to
understand the functions and processes being evaluated; and
5. Be willing to examine and evaluate the implemented CdM LMS.
Limitations of the Study
The system will depend on suitable devices, network access, and the availability of its
backend services. Cross-platform access does not imply identical capabilities, universal
operating-system support, uninterrupted service, or full offline operation. The exact instructor
functions available on mobile and the native coverage of the expanded coordination modules must
be documented against the version used for evaluation. The new coordination functions are planned
primarily for web access; native mobile parity is outside the stated release scope.
Academic analytics will describe available records and will not predict student outcomes.
CodeLab will assess submitted programs against predefined test cases; its results will not establish
complete program quality or constitute AI grading. Git repository history will support submission
review, but it will not independently prove authorship or eliminate plagiarism. Recorded assessment
events, such as tab switching or fullscreen exits, will be indicators for contextual review rather than
conclusive evidence of cheating.
Course scheduling will use Asia/Manila as its authoritative timezone. A weekly schedule
will use selected weekdays with a shared start and end time, date bounds, and related course
information. Effective-dated revisions will preserve timetable history. The release will not provide
arbitrary recurrence patterns, automatic holiday cancellation, room-conflict prevention, timetable
optimization, or automatic attendance. Overlapping classes may be displayed without being
automatically resolved. Student projection of recurring class timetables is outside this release;
students will retain applicable coursework deadlines and authorized saved events.
Course-supervision pages will exclude student identities, individual grades, submissions,
assessment attempts, answers, and teaching controls. The Super User will not receive grading,

coursework-submission, assessment-taking, security-management, backup-management, or generic
account-permission privileges. Dean and Program Head designations will remain distinct from the
four primary system roles.
Audience-targeted calendar dispatch will mean visibility within the LMS, without implying
external email, push delivery, or external-calendar synchronization. Converting a note to a calendar
event, or an accessible event to a personal note, will create a snapshot. Later changes to either item
will not continuously synchronize the copies. Generated class occurrences and coursework
deadlines will remain distinct from saved calendar events.
Optional grade incentives will be subject to applicable academic rules and confirmed
gradebook behavior. Their presence in the design will not imply institutional approval. Reporting,
monitoring, and backup and recovery coverage will be limited to functions demonstrated in the
evaluated version. Proposed additions will not be reported as completed or evaluated before
implementation and testing establish their status.
The study will assess software quality within the selected setting and tasks. It will not
determine long-term changes in grades, motivation, learning achievement, employability, or study
habits. Findings from purposively selected respondents will be interpreted within the ICS context
and will not represent all students or higher education institutions.
SIGNIFICANCE OF THE STUDY
The developed Colegio de Montalban Learning Management System (CdM LMS) is
significant to the Institute of Computing Studies (ICS) as it provides an integrated environment for
managing academic and technical learning activities across Web, Mobile, and Desktop platforms.
The study may provide value to the following:
Institute of Computing Studies and Colegio de Montalban. The study may provide an
institutional basis for organizing related academic information and examining whether a tailored

LMS meets the needs of ICS. Its documented requirements and evaluation findings may support
decisions about further development, maintenance, and possible adoption.
Students. The system is intended to provide a coordinated place for accessing coursework and
feedback and managing personal study activities. Students may benefit from clearer access to their
own academic information and opportunities for moderated peer support. These expected benefits
remain distinct from measured improvements in academic achievement.
Instructors. The study may support more consistent handling of course resources, submissions,
grading records, programming activities, and academic communication. Evaluation findings may
identify interaction or workflow difficulties that require correction before broader use.
Academic supervisors and Program Heads. The proposed coordination functions may support
authorized inspection of faculty and course information while preserving boundaries around student
records and teaching controls. A defined supervisory role may help clarify which information is
appropriate for academic coordination.
Administrators. The dedicated console is intended to support controlled account operations,
system records, reporting, and supported continuity functions. Documenting access boundaries and
audit behavior may assist in maintaining accountability for administrative actions.
Future researchers and developers. The study may provide a reference for examining an
institutional LMS with complementary applications, computing-specific workflows, and limited
academic supervision. Its limitations and evaluation findings may also identify questions requiring
separate research, including longer-term educational outcomes and broader platform coverage.
GENERAL FEATURES OF THE SYSTEM / STUDY
The CdM LMS is built to handle the technical needs of the ICS department composed of
interconnected Web, Mobile, and Desktop applications supported by a centralized database. The
system provides role-based functionality for students, instructors, and administrators while

maintaining synchronization of relevant academic and system information across its platforms. The
following are the general features of the implemented system.
Core Functional Features
Academic and Course Management
• Courses, Sections, and Enrollment: Authorized users create and organize courses and sections. Students
enter valid join codes to access their enrolled course workspaces.
• Course Workspace: Streams, classwork, people, and grades organize course information, activities,
membership, and permitted academic records.
• Learning Materials and Annotations: Instructors upload and organize resources. Users view supported
documents and add permitted highlights and sticky-note annotations.
• Assignments and Submissions: Instructors publish activities and deadlines. Students submit permitted
work, subject to submission validation and applicable deadline restrictions.
• Course Announcements: Instructors publish course updates for the authorized audience, with relevant
notifications available within the supported LMS workflow.
Grading and Academic Analytics
• Dynamic Gradebook: Instructors configure assessment components and weights, record scores, and obtain
automatically computed grades using the configured grading rules.
• Student Grade View: Students view their own authorized grade information and available progress
summaries.
• Visual Grade Analytics: Charts summarize existing grade and performance records for authorized students
and instructors.
• CSV Grade Export: Instructors export permitted grade records for their assigned courses.
Programming and Collaborative Learning

• CodeLab: Students write, execute, and submit code in the browser. Instructors manage programming
problems and predefined test cases used for assessment.
• Git-Integrated Submissions: Students submit applicable repository-based coursework for instructor review.
Any repository authorization is handled separately from LMS login.
• Knowledge Exchange: Students post academic and technical questions, contribute answers, and share
learning resources in a moderated environment.
• Faculty-Verified Answers and Reputation: Authorized instructors verify suitable answers and moderate
content. Configured contribution activity earns reputation points separately from EXP.
Personal Study and Gamification
• Notes and Tasks: Users organize personal notes, task lists, and relevant academic reminders within the
available client functions.
• Flashcards and Review: Students create and review flashcards, with configured review and mastery records
supporting repeated study.
• Focus and Study Tracking: Focus timers and study-session records allow students to record and review
their study activity.
• EXP, Levels, and Achievements: Eligible participation earns configured EXP and progression rewards,
including levels, achievements, badges, and streaks.
• Department Leaderboards and Rewards: Students view permitted participation rankings. Instructors
manage supported rewards; optional grade incentives remain subject to applicable academic rules.
Academic Coordination and Calendar
• Faculty Directory and Organizational Chart: Authorized users view faculty relationships, program
affiliations, and Dean and Program Head designations. Faculty classification remains separate from course
program classification.

• Academic Operations Hub: Super Users access authorized academic summaries, faculty filters, timetable
information, permitted leadership assignments, and shared faculty announcements.
• Restricted Course Supervision: Authorized academic supervisors view permitted course metadata,
instructor attribution, timetable, announcements, syllabus, and material summaries. Student identities,
individual grades, submissions, attempts, answers, and teaching controls remain excluded.
• Weekly Schedules and Revision History: Authorized instructors and Administrators manage course
schedules using selected weekdays, shared start and end times, date bounds, and Asia/Manila time.
Effective-dated revisions preserve timetable history.
• Class Exceptions: Authorized users cancel, reschedule, or restore permitted future class occurrences
without rewriting the entire recurring schedule.
• Calendar Views: Day, Week, Month, and Year views display authorized saved events, generated class
occurrences, and coursework deadlines as distinct record types. Student recurring timetable projection is
outside the stated release.
• Audience-Targeted Events: Saved events use Personal, Course, Institute Faculty, BSIT Instructors, or
BSCpE Instructors audiences. Program Heads may publish to permitted faculty audiences; publication rights
do not grant ownership of another creator’s content.
• Note–Event Snapshot Conversion: Users schedule an owned note as a private event or save an accessible
event as a private note. The new item preserves accessible content at conversion time rather than
continuously synchronizing later edits.
User Features
Role-Based Workspaces
• Student Workspace: Students access enrolled coursework, submit permitted activities, view personal
grades, participate in Knowledge Exchange, and use available study tools.

• Instructor Workspace: Instructors manage assigned courses, materials, assessments, grades, submissions,
and relevant academic communication. Mobile functions follow the coverage of the evaluated release.
• Super User Workspace: Super Users perform permitted academic oversight and coordination through the
web, with access to their own private notes and events. Academic oversight does not grant teaching, grading,
or generic administration privileges.
• Administrator Console: Administrators use the native Desktop Application for account approval, account
status and roles, subject assignments, directories, department configuration, logs, reports, and supported
continuity functions. Only Administrators provision or revoke Super User accounts.
• Program Head Designation: Eligible Instructor accounts receive defined program coordination
responsibilities. Dean and Program Head remain academic designations rather than additional primary
system roles.
System Capabilities
Cross-Platform Foundations
• Login and Registration: Users register and sign in through credential-based authentication. Verification and
Administrator approval govern access to the assigned account role.
• Home Dashboard: The role-appropriate landing view presents available summaries, such as student
progress and tasks, instructor course information, academic oversight summaries, or administrative status.
• Shared Data and Synchronization: The applicable Web, Mobile, and Desktop workflows use a shared
information environment. Saved updates become available to other authorized interfaces through backend
retrieval or synchronization, subject to connectivity and implemented update behavior.
• Automated Academic Processing: The system computes configured grades and progression values,
generates applicable calendar occurrences, and filters information according to the user’s permissions.
• In-LMS Updates: Relevant course and deadline notifications support academic tasks. Audience-targeted
calendar dispatch controls LMS visibility without implying external email, push delivery, or
external-calendar synchronization.

• Platform Help: An in-app help chatbot provides navigation and platform assistance.
Technology Integration
Connected Applications and Data Services
• Web Portal: The principal application supports academic workflows and the proposed coordination
environment.
• Mobile Application: The complementary client supports selected academic and productivity functions
according to role and release coverage.
• Desktop Application: The native Administrator Console supports permitted technical administration.
• Shared Backend and Database: Next.js backend services and a centralized PostgreSQL database connect
the authorized applications and maintain applicable records.
• Programming Workflow Integration: Repository-based coursework and CodeLab connect to their
respective academic activities. Supported providers, execution languages, and client technologies will follow
the implementation documented in Chapter 3.
Security Features
Account and Information Protection
• Verified Account Access: Credential authentication, account verification, registration approval, and
account-status controls govern LMS access.
• Server-Enforced Permissions: The backend checks session, role, institute, ownership, enrollment, and
related-resource permissions before allowing actions or returning restricted information.
• Academic Privacy: Personal grades, notes, restricted records, and audience-targeted content remain
accessible only through permitted workflows.

• Activity and Audit Records: Designated actions and changes are recorded to support administrative
accountability, academic coordination review, and moderation oversight.
• Record Integrity: Database constraints, transactions, and version checks in the proposed expansion protect
related records and concurrent updates.
• Repository Authorization: Access to applicable repositories follows its separately implemented
authorization mechanism and does not replace general LMS authentication.
Unique or Innovative Features
ICS Workflow Integration
• Complementary Platform Responsibilities: Academic access, selected mobile support, and desktop
administration operate around shared information with distinct role permissions.
• Computing Coursework Support: Separate CodeLab and Git-submission workflows support the different
requirements of execution-based activities and repository-based coursework.
• Connected Learning Support: Course information, personal study tools, gamified progression, and
moderated academic collaboration are organized within the ICS environment.
• Bounded Academic Oversight: A distinct Super User role supports coordination while restricted
supervision preserves the boundary between academic leadership, teaching, and system administration.
• Schedule and Calendar Coordination: Revision history, occurrence exceptions, targeted events, and private
snapshot conversion connect academic coordination and personal organization under defined access rules.
These features describe the proposed integration for ICS; their presence does not establish that comparable
capabilities are absent from other configurable LMS products.

DEFINITION OF TERMS
The following terms are operationally defined according to their use in this study and are arranged
alphabetically.
Academic Calendar - The interface presenting authorized saved events, generated class
occurrences, and coursework deadlines through Day, Week, Month, and Year views.
Academic Operations Hub - The web interface through which a Super User views authorized
academic summaries, faculty information, timetable filters, and course-supervision links.
Administrator - The system role responsible for authorized account, permission, configuration,
log, reporting, and continuity operations through the native Administrator Console.
Agile Development - The iterative development approach in which requirements are implemented,
tested, reviewed, and refined through successive project cycles.
Audit Log - A record of designated actions and changes used to support accountability, including
authorized administrative and academic-leadership operations.
CdM LMS - The proposed interconnected learning management environment developed for the
Institute of Computing Studies at Colegio de Montalban.
Centralized Database - The shared PostgreSQL data store supporting authorized academic and
system records used by the applicable applications.
CodeLab - The in-browser programming environment for writing, executing, and submitting code
assessed against predefined test cases.
Course Supervision - Restricted, read-only access to course metadata, instructor attribution,
timetable, announcements, syllabus, and learning-material summaries.
Dynamic Gradebook - The grading module that uses configured components, weights, and
recorded scores to compute and display authorized grade information.

Effective Date - The date from which a particular timetable revision governs the generation of
applicable recurring class occurrences.
Experience Points or EXP - Configured participation points used for gamified progression and
related rewards; they are not equivalent to course grades or forum reputation.
Faculty Directory - The authorized listing of ICS faculty, program affiliations, leadership
designations, and relevant assigned-course summaries.
Faculty-Verified Answer - A Knowledge Exchange response marked by authorized faculty
through the platform’s answer-verification process.
Gamification - The use of configured points, levels, badges, achievements, streaks, and
leaderboards to support participation in permitted LMS activities.
Git-Integrated Submission Engine - The workflow for repository-based coursework submission
and authorized instructor review of applicable programming activities.
Institute of Computing Studies or ICS - The institute at Colegio de Montalban that defines the
development context and research-evaluation scope of the study.
Instructor - The system role responsible for authorized teaching, assessment, grading, and
course-related communication for assigned courses.
Knowledge Exchange - The moderated environment for academic and technical questions,
answers, and resource sharing, with faculty verification and reputation mechanisms.
Learning Management System or LMS - The application environment used in this study to
organize course resources, coursework, assessment, academic records, and related support
workflows.

Program Head - An academic designation attached to an eligible ICS Instructor account for a
specified program, with defined coordination privileges.
Reputation Points - Configured points associated with Knowledge Exchange contributions,
maintained distinctly from EXP unless an explicit rule connects them.
Role-Based Access Control or RBAC - The mechanism that restricts system capabilities
according to assigned roles, supplemented by institute, ownership, enrollment, and related-resource
checks.
Schedule Exception - A record modifying an individual class occurrence through cancellation or
rescheduling, or supporting restoration of its original occurrence.
Snapshot Conversion - Creation of a private note or calendar event from accessible source content
at the time of conversion, without continuous synchronization.
Spaced-Repetition-Oriented Review - Flashcard review organized to support repeated study over
time, without assuming an unverified scheduling algorithm.
Student - The system role permitted to access enrolled-course content, submit assigned work, view
authorized personal academic records, and use available learning-support functions.
Super User - The system role for limited academic oversight and coordination, separate from
Instructor and Administrator privileges.
Targeted Event - A saved academic event whose visibility and management are governed by its
designated personal, course, institute-faculty, or program-instructor audience.
Timetable Revision - An effective-dated version of a course schedule used to preserve the
historical representation of recurring class times.
Visual Grade Analytics - Descriptive charts and summaries derived from available grade and
performance records, without predictive or AI-based inference.

CHAPTER 2: REVIEW OF RELATED LITERATURES
Digital technology has changed how educational institutions organize instruction and
manage academic information. Learning Management Systems (LMS) provide a shared
environment for distributing course materials, managing assignments, recording grades, and
communicating with students. Access through different devices also creates opportunities to
connect classroom activities with independent study. These functions provide the foundation for
examining how an LMS can support academic work within higher education.
In the Philippine context, the studies reviewed in this chapter examine LMS adoption, user
experience, accessibility, and institutional support. They also explore programming practice,
gamification, personal learning strategies, and online collaboration. Their findings provide different
perspectives on digital learning, including the difficulties users encounter and the conditions that
support meaningful participation. Understanding these findings helps guide the selection and
integration of functions appropriate to the Institute of Computing Studies (ICS) at Colegio de
Montalban.
The project developers reviewed scholarly articles, conference papers, and system-based
studies to establish the foundation for the proposed Learning Management System. Philippine and
international studies are organized under seven topics: Multi-Platform Learning Management
Systems; Course Management and Academic Communication; Programming Practice and
Automated Assessment; Git-Based Coursework Submission; Gamification and Student
Engagement; Personal Study Tools and Self-Regulated Learning; and Online Collaboration and
Knowledge Sharing. The discussion compares their findings, explains their connection to the
proposed system, and identifies the research gap that the study will address.

2.1.1 Multi-Platform Learning Management Systems
Access through different devices should support useful academic tasks and an
understandable learning environment. Alfalah (2023) surveyed 258 students from Hail University,
Aljouf University, and Northern Border University in Saudi Arabia about mobile LMS adoption,
including the Blackboard application. Performance expectancy, effort expectancy, and learning
intention were associated with behavioral intention to use the system. In the Philippines, Dela Rosa
(2023) examined Canvas Free for Teachers with 132 third-year BSIT students taking Web Systems
and Technologies 2 at Bulacan State University. Students evaluated its lesson modules and
assessments favorably. Both studies connect adoption with users' experiences of academic
functions, although Alfalah examined mobile-use intentions and Dela Rosa examined acceptance
within a specific programming course.
Philippine development studies provide more direct examples of designing learning access
across devices. Quimod et al. (2023) developed e-Modyul, a mobile and web LMS for
Technical-Vocational-Livelihood education, and evaluated it with 10 teachers and 20 students. Its
approach supports accessing lessons and assessments through different operating systems. Ramos et
al. (2024), researchers associated with the University of the Philippines Open University (UPOU),
developed a Filipinized LMS responsive to Filipino nursing educators and learners. Their design
considered connectivity limitations, multimodal learning materials, communication, and
collaboration. These studies share an emphasis on access, but e-Modyul focuses on device
coverage, while the Filipinized LMS emphasizes adaptation to its users and educational context.
Platform access also depends on the quality of everyday workflows. Llamas et al. (2025)
examined the Moodle-based LMS at Mindanao State University–Iligan Institute of Technology
(MSU–IIT), involving six academics and six fourth-year students. They identified concerns in
usability, communication, course building, monitoring and assessment, content management, and
technical support. Their findings qualify the favorable acceptance evidence from Dela Rosa:
providing an LMS does not remove all difficulties in using it.

Taken together, these five studies support designing complementary interfaces around the
tasks and access conditions of the intended users. For CdM LMS, the web application will provide
the principal academic environment, the mobile application will support selected student and
instructor functions, and the desktop application will serve the Administrator. Multi-platform access
therefore concerns coordinated responsibilities and consistent shared records rather than identical
functionality on every device. The reviewed studies inform this arrangement, while its suitability
for ICS will require evaluation of the implemented applications.
2.1.2 Course Management and Academic Communication
Course management connects learning materials, activities, academic records, and
communication within a clear workflow. Peralta (2024) developed a course management system for
Centro Escolar University and evaluated it with 100 students and eight faculty members. It
organized materials, announcements, assignments, quizzes, and grades and included Short
Messaging Service notifications. Llamas et al. (2025), however, identified course-building,
content-management, communication, and assessment concerns in the MSU–IIT LMS. These
studies suggest that organizing functions within one platform is useful, but users must still be able
to complete their tasks without unnecessary difficulty.
The communication experience also varies across educational settings. Acala and Dimasacat
(2023) examined perceptions of 74 private senior high school students in Manila and reported
favorable views of LMS-supported interaction and learning. They recommended training to help
students and teachers use the available functions. Laspiñas and Almerez (2024), in contrast,
surveyed 33 business graduate students at an unnamed university in Cebu City and reported
generally neutral evaluations of the LMS's pragmatic and hedonic qualities. Their findings address
different populations, yet both indicate that communication and task support should be assessed
through users' experiences rather than inferred from the presence of features.

Institutional support affects whether these workflows can be maintained. Guico (2026)
examined 182 faculty members and 29 administrators from 11 higher education institutions in
Batangas, including Batangas State University, Lipa City College, and Rizal College of Taal.
Reported concerns included preparation time, resistance to change, access to information and
communication technology resources, and continuing training. Francisco (2026) examined remote
learning management at the University of Rizal System and likewise identified connectivity,
digital-resource, technological-competence, engagement, and assessment-integrity challenges. Both
studies place course management within a wider environment of faculty support and institutional
coordination.
Across these six studies, effective academic communication depends on understandable
course organization, appropriate user preparation, and the support needed to sustain the system.
This evidence informs CdM's course materials, announcements, submissions, feedback, dynamic
grading, and descriptive grade analytics. It also supports considering faculty organization,
schedules, and targeted academic events as part of course coordination. Peralta's SMS function
remains a comparison feature of that system; the proposed CdM workflow uses its own documented
notification functions. Requirements gathering at ICS will establish the local difficulties to be
addressed.
2.1.3 Programming Practice and Automated Assessment
Programming practice requires suitable exercises and feedback that explains performance
against clear criteria. Messer et al. (2024) reviewed 121 papers on automated grading and feedback
tools for programming education. Many tools evaluated correctness through dynamic methods such
as unit tests, while readability, maintainability, and documentation received less attention. Novak
and Kermek (2024), from the University of Zagreb in Croatia, examined automation for complex
programming assignments using unit testing and custom scripts. Both studies support automating
selected checks while retaining instructor judgment for aspects that those checks cannot adequately
assess.

Philippine research adds considerations about introductory practice and access. Asuncion et
al. (2022), affiliated with Ateneo de Manila University and the National Olympiad in
Informatics–Philippines, presented the ABC Workbook and AutoJudge++. The project combines
introductory Python exercises with an offline desktop checker that compares outputs against test
cases. Classroom effectiveness evaluation remained future work. Arada (2025) examined Tinkercad
with 42 first-year Computer Technology students at a Philippine state university. The platform
received a below-average System Usability Scale score of 58, despite many students expressing
willingness to use it. These studies concern different tools, but together they show that opportunities
to practice should be considered alongside exercise design, usability, and access conditions.
Assessment can also concern development processes beyond the output of an individual
program. Fernandez-Gauna et al. (2023), from the University of the Basque Country in Spain,
described automated feedback and assessment for team-coding assignments in a DevOps context.
Their approach used team and individual indicators and periodic reports to support monitoring.
Compared with the test-case approaches examined by Messer et al. and Asuncion et al., this work
illustrates a broader form of assessment involving collaborative development activity. It does not
establish that development indicators can replace assessment of the submitted program.
The five studies support matching automated feedback to the assignment and preserving the
limits of what is measured. CdM's CodeLab will evaluate programming work against predefined
test cases and provide understandable results. Its checks will concern documented expected
behavior rather than complete program quality. Git-based coursework review will remain a separate
workflow. The related studies therefore guide test design, feedback presentation, and usability
without expanding CodeLab into automated code repair, artificial intelligence grading, or
DevOps-based team assessment.

2.1.4 Git-Based Coursework Submission
Repository-based coursework can connect code submissions with an organized record of
development and instructor review. Schauer et al. (2024), from Heriot-Watt University in the United
Kingdom, developed a framework integrating Canvas LMS and GitLab. They identified fragmented
information and poor user experiences when the platforms were used independently and
implemented eight applications to connect their workflows. Orvalho et al. (2024), affiliated with the
University of Lisbon and Czech Technical University in Prague, presented GitSEED, a
GitLab-backed automated assessment tool. Both approaches connect academic work with version
control, although Schauer et al. emphasize LMS integration and GitSEED provides assessment and
feedback through repository workflows.
Evidence about students' use of repositories complements these system-development
approaches. Patani et al. (2024) examined GitHub use in a software engineering course with 319
undergraduate students, using surveys and repository records such as commits, pull requests, and
issues. They reported improvements in collaborative development and teamwork after the course
experience. Fernandez-Gauna et al. (2023) used repository-related development indicators to
provide feedback on team-coding assignments. Together, these studies show how repositories can
make development activity available for educational review, but their measures extend beyond
recording a final coursework submission.
Philippine evidence places GitHub within a wider teaching approach. Bernardez et al.
(2026), from the University of the Philippines Cebu, examined Design Thinking and Agile-Scrum
across two software engineering courses involving 65 students. Their findings describe GitHub and
Trello as supporting version control and task coordination, alongside challenges involving time
pressure and uneven workloads. Since GitHub formed part of a combined instructional approach,
the study cannot isolate its contribution to learning outcomes. It nevertheless demonstrates the use
of repository tools in Philippine computing coursework.

These five studies support examining how academic instructions, repository records, and
instructor feedback can be connected. For CdM LMS, Git authorization will support the
documented repository submission and review process, while LMS account access will follow its
separate authentication and approval rules. Repository submissions will not automatically become
CodeLab assessments or commit-based academic grades. The project's contribution is to evaluate
its particular coursework workflow for ICS, informed by the integration concerns identified by
Schauer et al. and the educational repository use described in the other studies.
2.1.5 Gamification and Student Engagement
Gamification can encourage participation when rewards are connected to meaningful
learning activities. Ahmed et al. (2025) evaluated a gamified, mobile, cloud-based LMS with 60
second-year students taking Object-Oriented Programming at Mansoura University in Egypt. The
experimental group obtained higher post-test achievement and engagement scores than the
comparison group. Jaramillo-Mediavilla et al. (2024) synthesized gamification research and
reported favorable findings in parts of the literature while identifying gaps in examining motivation
and academic performance together. These studies support investigating gamification, but the
outcomes of a particular intervention should not be treated as a guaranteed effect of every reward
system.
The design of participation incentives matters. Jack et al. (2025) examined points and
leaderboards in a flipped statistics classroom and discussed benefits for motivation and engagement
alongside the risks of superficial engagement and demotivation. Philippine evidence from Fojas
(2022) examined gamification in Moodle courses at UPOU, comparing a gamified cohort with
earlier non-gamified cohorts and collecting student feedback. The reported differences favored the
gamified course, but forum-grading arrangements also differed between cohorts, and some students
described anxiety or limited interest in rewards. Both studies show why participation counts and
positive feedback need to be interpreted in relation to the design of the activities.

Benben and Bug-os (2022) studied Quizizz-based formative assessment with Grade 10
physics students at Central Mindanao University Laboratory High School in Bukidnon.
Achievement and motivation increased after the intervention, although the reported learning gain
was low. Its one-group pretest-posttest design and secondary-school setting differ from Ahmed et
al.'s computing-course comparison. The studies therefore provide complementary evidence about
possible motivational benefits while leaving questions about transfer to other subjects and
populations.
Across these five studies, gamification is most relevant when its rules encourage
participation without obscuring academic expectations. CdM LMS will use EXP, levels,
achievements, streaks, and leaderboards under defined rules. These records will remain separate
from academic grades and Knowledge Exchange reputation. The literature supports the rationale for
these mechanisms and the need to examine users' experiences, while the proposed descriptive
software-quality evaluation will not establish their long-term causal effects on achievement or
motivation.
2.1.6 Personal Study Tools and Self-Regulated Learning
Personal study tools can support planning, active review, and reflection when learners use
them purposefully. Du et al. (2025) examined an LMS enhanced with self-regulated learning
support among 69 management undergraduates taking mathematics at an unnamed large public
university in China. Students reported stronger self-regulation, but an examination advantage
appeared on the first test and not the second. Heikkinen et al. (2023), in a review of 56 studies,
found that only 46 percent of the reviewed learning-analytics interventions reported positive effects
on learning. Both studies indicate that learning support deserves investigation, while access to
monitoring tools alone does not ensure improved outcomes.
Students' interactions with LMS tools help explain differences in how learning support is
used. Çakiroğlu et al. (2024) examined a third-year Operating Systems and Applications course at

an unnamed public university in Turkey. They identified different learner profiles and relationships
between assessment interactions and self-regulation skills, including goal setting, self-evaluation,
and help-seeking. In the Philippines, Funa et al. (2023) surveyed 301 preservice teachers in the
Bicol region and supplemented the survey with interviews. Participants reported relatively strong
environment structuring and goal setting but also difficulties with task strategies, time allocation,
priorities, and interaction. These studies connect self-regulation with both individual learning
practices and the conditions in which academic tasks are completed.
Active review provides another form of personal learning support. Pan et al. (2023)
compared user-generated and premade digital flashcards in six experiments involving delayed tests.
Creating flashcard content generally supported memory and, in several conditions, application
performance. Unlike the broader LMS and analytics studies, this research examines a specific
review activity. It offers a direct basis for considering student-created flashcards alongside the
organization and reflection functions discussed by Du et al., Çakiroğlu et al., and Funa et al.
Together, the five studies support making planning, review, and progress information
available within the learning environment. For CdM LMS, personal notes, tasks, flashcards, review
and mastery records, and focus-study records will provide ways to organize and revisit academic
work. Descriptive displays can help users inspect their saved records, but their presence will not be
treated as evidence of improved self-regulation. The implemented functions will require evaluation
for usability and correct behavior, while their educational effects remain a possible direction for
later research.
2.1.7 Online Collaboration and Knowledge Sharing
Online knowledge sharing depends on the quality of interaction and the way discussions are
organized. Oyarzun and Martin (2023) reviewed 63 studies on online learner collaboration and
examined technologies, instructional design, facilitation, and outcomes. Their review connects
collaboration with the conditions supporting participation. Bach and Thiel (2024) surveyed 298

undergraduate teacher-education students in asynchronous university courses and examined
cognitive, metacognitive, and relational dimensions of interaction. Their findings concern
associations with self-reported learning gains and satisfaction rather than causal effects. Both
studies indicate that a shared online space should be assessed through the exchanges it supports.
Structured discussions and instructor involvement provide more specific guidance. Mudau
and Van den Berg (2023), from the University of South Africa, examined online discussions
involving 11 master's students in education. They identified the importance of clear guidelines,
structured questions, and opportunities for discussion within a community of inquiry. Almodiel
(2022) analyzed knowledge construction in asynchronous discussions within a graduate colloquium
at UPOU. The study used the Interaction Analysis Model to examine the exchanges through which
learners shared and developed knowledge. These studies support considering discussion structure
and facilitation alongside opportunities for students to contribute.
Participation measures should also reflect interaction between users. Kumi (2023) examined
discussion-forum exchanges in an undergraduate class with 31 students using social network
analysis. The analysis revealed structural and relational aspects of participation that simple counts
or self-reports could overlook. This complements Almodiel's examination of knowledge
construction: both approaches look beyond the number of messages to consider how students
interact. Their analytical methods are research approaches rather than functions automatically
required in the proposed CdM system.
The five studies support designing Knowledge Exchange as an organized space for
academic questions, answers, and resource sharing. Moderation and Faculty-Verified Answers will
provide project-specific ways to manage contributions and identify instructor-reviewed responses.
Reputation will describe forum participation under its configured rules and remain separate from
EXP and academic grades. The literature provides reasons to examine participation, facilitation, and
contribution quality, while the suitability of CdM's verification and reputation mechanisms will

require its own evaluation. The proposed forum supports asynchronous exchanges; the reviewed
studies do not require adding live meetings or collaborative document editing.
2.2 Supporting Quality Framework and Local Study Context
ISO/IEC 25010:2023 provides the product-quality model supporting the study's selected
evaluation characteristics: functional suitability, interaction capability, security, performance
efficiency, reliability, and compatibility (International Organization for Standardization, 2023). The
standard is a supporting framework rather than one of the five studies counted within each topic.
Questionnaire feedback will describe respondents' evaluations, while calculation checks, access
tests, and integration verification will provide evidence about implemented behavior.
The reviewed Philippine studies provide context from computing courses, institutional LMS
use, programming practice, gamified learning, and online discussions. Francisco (2026) adds
evidence from the University of Rizal System, bringing access and coordination concerns closer to
the geographical setting of Colegio de Montalban. Findings from these institutions do not establish
the conditions within ICS. Requirements gathering and system evaluation will identify the needs
and experiences of the intended BSIT and BSCpE users.
2.3 Related Systems
The following systems provide documented examples of course organization, progress
information, and repository-based workflows. The comparison uses the capabilities described in the
cited sources rather than an exhaustive feature audit. It does not assume that these platforms lack
other functions or cannot be extended.
2.3.1 Moodle
Moodle's publication on LMS 4.5 described improvements to assignment interaction and
course subsections for organizing content (Moodle, 2024). Llamas et al. (2025) examined its
institutional use at MSU–IIT, while Fojas (2022) and Almodiel (2022) examined gamification and

discussions in the UPOU context. These sources show that Moodle can support several forms of
academic work. For CdM LMS, the relevant comparison concerns the organization of coursework
and the experience of completing institutional tasks.
2.3.2 Google Classroom
Mennuti (2024) described targeted assignments, rubrics, and analytics for grades,
completion rates, and missing work in Google Classroom. The analytics described were associated
with specified education editions or upgrades. These functions provide comparison points for
assignment management and descriptive progress information. Their documentation does not
establish the quality of the proposed CdM implementation or demonstrate that it will outperform
Classroom.
2.3.3 Canvas and GitLab Integration
Schauer et al. (2024) implemented a framework connecting Canvas and GitLab to reduce
fragmented workflows and support feedback. Its eight applications demonstrate that existing LMS
and version-control platforms can be connected for educational use. This is a direct comparison for
the integration concern in CdM's Git submission workflow. The technologies and automation
described in that framework remain distinct from CdM's specified implementation.
2.3.4 GitSEED
Orvalho et al. (2024) presented GitSEED as a GitLab-backed automated assessment tool
supporting programming and software engineering education. It uses repositories as part of
submission and feedback workflows. Its approach provides a comparison for connecting
coursework with version control, but its automated assessment capabilities extend beyond CdM's
separate repository-submission and instructor-review process.

2.5 Synthesis of the Literature
The literature connects LMS adoption with useful academic functions, understandable
interaction, and conditions supporting continued use. Alfalah (2023) and Dela Rosa (2023) address
acceptance, while Quimod et al. (2023), Ramos et al. (2024), and Llamas et al. (2025) provide
development and user-experience perspectives. Peralta (2024), Guico (2026), and Francisco (2026)
further connect coursework with communication and institutional support. These studies support
examining connected workflows and appropriate access across CdM's complementary applications.
Programming and repository research address related but distinct academic processes.
Messer et al. (2024), Asuncion et al. (2022), and Novak and Kermek (2024) inform checks against
